catalog_quote: [Kato 2003 p.633-634] The syllable structure of the Hpa-an dialect can be represented as C1(C2)V1(V2)(C3)/T, where C1 is an onset consonant, C2 is the second member of a cluster, V is a vowel, C3 is a coda, and T is a tone. ... There are four tones: High-level ... Pronounced with normal voice. Mid-level ... Pronounced with breathy voice. It is sometimes accompanied by arising contour especially in utterance final position. Low-level ... Pronounced with normal voice. Falling ... Pronounced with slightly creaky voice. ... The Hpa-an dialect has atonic syllables, in which /ə/ is the only permitted vowel, and which never occur in utterance final position. [Kato 2004 sec. 2.5-2.6] ポー・カレン語の声調素には次に掲げる四つがある。... 高平調 ... 中平調 ... 低平調 ... 下降調 ... ポー・カレン語には声調を持たない音節がある。これを軽声音節 (atonic syllable) と呼ぶ。表記上は、声調符号を付さないことによってこれを示す。軽声音節に現れる母音は、/ə/ のみである。軽声音節が発話末に現れることは決してない。... tone_statements.citation: 加藤昌彦 [Kato, Atsuhiko]. 2022. 東部ポー・カレン語入門 (2022年度版) [Introduction to Eastern Pwo Karen, 2022 edition]. Course text with accompanying audio recordings (PwoPrimerRecording.zip), posted on the author's Keio University page:http://user.keio.ac.jp/~kato/PwoKarenPrimer.pdf
tone_statements.quote: 声調 /á/ [55]: /khá/「苦い」, /má/「誤った」, /bá/「正しい」 /ā/: [33~334] /khā/「折れる」, /phā/「父」, /mʊ̄/「母」 /à/: [11] /ɣà/「～人」, /thà/「針」, /mà/「する」, /nà/「夜」 /â/: [51] /mâ/「妻」, /châ/「痛い」, /jɔ̂/「易しい」 … 下降調を持つ 2,3,6,7 の声調が中平調に交替することに注意。ただし正書法上は元の下降調を表す綴り字で書かれる。
tone_statements.translation: Tones. /á/ [55]: /khá/ 'bitter', /má/ 'wrong', /bá/ 'correct'; /ā/ [33~334]: /khā/ 'break', /phā/ 'father', /mʊ̄/ 'mother'; /à/ [11]: /ɣà/ 'classifier for persons', /thà/ 'needle', /mà/ 'do', /nà/ 'night'; /â/ [51]: /mâ/ 'wife', /châ/ 'hurt', /jɔ̂/ 'easy' … Note that the tone of 2, 3, 6, 7, which have the falling tone, alternates to the mid level tone. In the orthography, however, they are written with the spelling for the original falling tone.
tone_statements.locator: p.2, section 'ポー・カレン語東部方言の発音' > '声調'; alternation note in Lesson 7 '位を表す数詞' (txt l.981-983)
tone_statements.summary: Four tones: high level [55], mid level [33~334], low [11], falling [51]; the falling tone of numerals 2, 3, 6, 7 becomes mid before classifiers and before 'ten', 'hundred' etc. Nothing on word stress.

tone_statements.citation: Luangthongkum, Theraphan. 2019. A View on Proto-Karen Phonology and Lexicon. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (ISSN 1836-6823), 52 pp. University of Hawai'i Press / eVols,http://hdl.handle.net/10524/52441.
tone_statements.quote: Most or all of the Pho varieties have four tones in non-checked syllables, i.e. PK *A > A1-23 and PK *B > B12-3. The unusual split pattern in the A-tone column is useful for the reconstruction of some glottalised sonorants. The phonetic characteristics or tone shapes of the A1, A23, B12, B3, D12 and D3 tones in N.Pwo and S.Pwo are different: 35, 55, 33 and 11¨ in N.Pwo and 53, 31¨, 55 and 33 in S.Pwo, respectively. … N. Pwo S. Pwo *A *B *D *A *B *D 1 35 33 45’ 1 53 55 21’ 2 55 33 45’ 2 31¨ 55 21’ 3 55 11¨ 21’ 3 31¨ 33 45’

tone_statements.summary: For Southern Pwo of Uthai Thani, Thailand (not Hpa-an): four tones in non-checked syllables, 53, 31, 55, 33 (= A1, A23, B12, B3), plus 21 and 45 in checked syllables; author's own field wordlists.

tone_statements.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2018. How did Haudricourt reconstruct Proto-Karen tones? Reports of the Keio Institute of Cultural and Linguistic Studies 49: 21-44. (Author PDF:http://user.keio.ac.jp/~kato/ProtoKarenTones.pdf;Japanese version; first read at the International Seminar on Languages and Linguistics in Middle Mekong Region, Kobe, 2018-01-06.)
tone_statements.quote: The Hpa-an dialect has four tones: /má/[55] (high-level), /mā/[33(4)] (mid-level), /mà/[11] (low-level), /mâ/[51] (falling) (see Kato 1995, 2009, 2017). … Originally, the tonal signs from ‘1’ to ‘4’ indicated plain tones, and ‘5’ and ‘6’ indicated the checked tones that had a glottal stop at the end. In the Hpa-an dialect, however, the final glottal stop has recently been dropped and the original checked tones ‘5’ and ‘6’ are merged with the plain tones ‘1’ and ‘3’ respectively.
tone_statements.locator: p. 25, section 1, text under Table 1 'Tonal signs of Christian Pwo Karen Script'; pitch values by proto-category in Table 8 'Tones of Pwo (Hpa-an)', p. 39
tone_statements.summary: Four tones in Hpa-an Pwo Karen: high-level [55], mid-level [33], low-level [11], falling [51]; the two former checked tones lost the final glottal stop and merged with high and low.

tone_statements.citation: Phillips, Audra. 2018. West-Central Thailand Pwo Karen Phonology. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (ISSN 1836-6823), 16 pp. University of Hawai'i Press / eVols,http://hdl.handle.net/10524/52420.
tone_statements.quote: The WCT Pwo tonal system consists of four modal tones and two glottalized tones, which exhibit final glottal closure. All six tones are contour tones. Thus, the IPA word accent marks are used just to label the tones and do not indicate the nature of the tone. … The six phonemic tones of WCT Pwo are detailed in Table 5. … Table 5: WCT Pwo tonemes Tone name Tone symbol Tone numbers High rise /ɐ́/ 45 Mid rise /ɐ̃̄/ 34 Low falling /ɐ̀/ 21 High falling /ɐ̃̂/ 51 High glottalized /ɐ́ˀ/ 45ˀ Low glottalized /ɐ̀ˀ/ 21ˀ
tone_statements.locator: pp. 53-54, sec. 2.3 'Tone and intonation' with Table 5 'WCT Pwo tonemes'; Hpa-an comparison pp. 59-60, sec. 4, Table 8
tone_statements.summary: West-Central Thailand Pwo: six contour tones, four modal (45, 34, 21, 51) and two glottalized (45ˀ, 21ˀ), on major syllables; Hpa-an Eastern Pwo has the four modal tones only, glottalized lost.

tone_statements.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2009 [printed 2010]. A basic vocabulary of Htoklibang Pwo Karen with Hpa-an, Kyonbyaw, and Proto-Pwo Karen forms. tone_statements.quote: 3.1. The Hpa-an dialect The phonemes and all of the rhymes of the Hpa-an dialect are shown in Table 8. Table 8 Hpa-an phonemes and rhymes … Tones … má [55] … mā [33∼334] … mà [11] … mâ [51] … (m@ atonic) … • The tone /ā/ is pronounced with a breathy phonation. It may be pronounced with a rising pitch in the utterance-final position and before a pause. • The tone /â/ is pronounced with a creaky phonation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 177, sec. 3.1 'The Hpa-an dialect', Table 8 'Hpa-an phonemes and rhymes'; see also Table 5 'Hpa-an (Eastern)' p. 175 and Table 14 'Correspondences of tones' p. 181
tone_statements.summary: Four tones in the Hpa-an dialect: high 55, mid 33~334 (breathy, may rise before pause), low 11, falling 51 (creaky); plus atonic schwa syllables. Author's own field data.

tone_statements.translation: [Sec. 3 intro:] The tone patterns of syllables pronounced in isolation are shown. … 3.4. Pwo Karen, Hpa-an dialect (after Kato [1995]). Spoken in Hpa-an town, Karen State, Union of Burma. It is thought that there used to be tones ending in a glottal stop, but at present they have merged into the high-level and low-level [tones]. … high level [55] /kha55/ 'bitter', /ja55/ 'be torn'; mid level [33] /pha33/ 'father'; low level [11] /ma11/ 'do', /tha11/ 'iron'; falling [51] /cha51/ 'hurt'.
tone_statements.locator: printed: sec. ３ 現代カレン諸方言の声調 intro (foot of p.2), ３．４ ポー・カレン語パアン(Hpa-an)方言 heading and prose (foot of p.3), four-tone chart (top of p.4)
tone_statements.summary: Hpa-an Pwo Karen has four tones on syllables in isolation: high level 55, mid level 33, low level 11 and falling 51; earlier glottal-stop-final tones have merged into the high and low level tones.

audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal; no word-stress rule; domain unstated) rests on the 603-page reference grammar of exactly this dialect by its principal describer (Kato 2004), held held by the project, with the deciding Japanese passage confirmed verbatim at pp. 21-23 (secs 2.5-2.6) and the English cross-check (Kato 2003) confirmed in the djvu text we hold. I downloaded and read the remaining Kato phonology sources (1995 LTBA via scanned, 2019 Mouton preprint, 2021 Karenic typology preprint): all state four lexical tones on full syllables plus toneless /ə/-only atonic syllables that cannot be utterance-final, and none posits a word-stress or accent rule; Kato 2021 merely glosses atonal syllables as 'phonetically unstressed and short' and sesquisyllables as unstressed+stressed, which is the full-vs-minor asymmetry the record already describes. The only source with a stress section is Phillips 2000 on West-Central Tha

sources.quote: 'There are four tonemes in the Hpa-an dialect: high-level [55], mid-level [33], low-level [11], falling [51] ... accompanied by laryngealization'; 'The Hpa-an dialect has atonic syllables, in which /ə/ is the only permitted vowel, and which never occur in utterance final position.' Only use of 'stress': numeral 'one' 'appears in the unstressed form /lə-/' before a classifier (p. 80). No stress/accent section.

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2021. Typological profile of Karenic languages. In P. Sidwell & M. Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, 337-367. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton (author preprint, ch. 18).
sources.quote: 'EPK (the Hpa-an dialect) has four tones'; 'EPK has atonal syllables, which are phonetically unstressed and short, and cannot occur utterance-finally ... The only vowel that can occur in an atonal syllable is /ə/ ... EPK has many disyllabic words that have an atonal first syllable. These are sesquisyllabic in Matisoff's (1973) terms, in that they are composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable.' Also: first syllables of some disyllables may reduce to atonal in rapid speech (/khʊ́lòɴ ~ khəlòɴ/ 'mountain').
sources.locator: sec. 18.2, preprint the text (EPK four tones) and 346-356 (atonal syllables)
sources.note: Most recent statement by the dialect authority; the only Kato text that uses the word 'stress' for Hpa-an (atonal syllables 'phonetically unstressed and short'; sesquisyllables = unstressed + stressed syllable) -- useful wording for the record's tone_note/caution, does not change the tonal coding.
sources.venue: The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia

sources.quote: For West-Central Thailand Pwo (Kanchanaburi; a different dialect under the same Glottolog languoid): 'Pwo Karen, for the most part, exhibits two rhythmic patterns in words. The first is the unstressed-stressed iambic pattern ... The other rhythmic pattern is combinations of major syllables where the first major syllable is stressed ... as in /mɨ mí/ sun'; atonic/proclitic [ə] morphemes are 'destressed variants ... due to the rhythmic patterns at the phrase and clause level'; 'As yet, evidence is limited on Pwo Karen rhythm'. Four phonemic tones (sec. 4.4.1). This is the account Kato 2004 sec.
sources.locator: sec. 3 'Stress and rhythm', p. 100 (page scan checked)
sources.note: The work Kato 2004 sec. 2.6 argues against; gives an explicit (impressionistic) word-rhythm statement for the Thailand Pwo variety grouped under the same glottocode (iambic minor+major; first-syllable stress in major+major words). Relevant if the catalog ever splits or annotates dialects; downloaded and read now.

sources.citation: Naruemon Chuensukon (1995). A phonological study of Pwo Karen at Huay-Hom-Nok Village, Tambon Th. Mahidol University.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The thesis describes the Pwo Karen of Huay-Hom-Nok Village, Lamphun Province, northern Thailand, i.e. a Northern Pwo Karen (Phlong) variety, not the Hpa-an dialect of Eastern Pwo Karen (Myanmar) that the catalog item pwoe1235 is named for. Glottolog attaches it to pwoe1235, which is why it was listed. For that Lamphun variety the statement is a clean fixed: final syllable rule (predictable, on the word-final major syllable, with secondary stress on minor syllables and zero on presyllables). The catalog record for pwoe1235 has an empty rule, so nothing is contradicted; if the catalog accepts T…

sources.quote: The WCT Pwo tonal system consists of four modal tones and two glottalized tones, which exhibit final glottal closure. All six tones are contour tones. Thus, the IPA word accent marks are used just to label the tones and do not indicate the nature of the tone. … The six phonemic tones of WCT Pwo are detailed in Table 5. … Table 5: WCT Pwo tonemes Tone name Tone symbol Tone numbers High rise /ɐ́/ 45 Mid rise /ɐ̃̄/ 34 Low falling /ɐ̀/ 21 High falling /ɐ̃̂/ 51 High glottalized /ɐ́ˀ/ 45ˀ Low glottalized /ɐ̀ˀ/ 21ˀ

tone.translation: [Sec. 3 intro:] The tone patterns of syllables pronounced in isolation are shown. … 3.4. Pwo Karen, Hpa-an dialect (after Kato [1995]). Spoken in Hpa-an town, Karen State, Union of Burma. It is thought that there used to be tones ending in a glottal stop, but at present they have merged into the high-level and low-level [tones]. … high level [55] /kha55/ 'bitter', /ja55/ 'be torn'; mid level [33] /pha33/ 'father'; low level [11] /ma11/ 'do', /tha11/ 'iron'; falling [51] /cha51/ 'hurt'.

sources.note: Survey word lists of four Central Thailand Pwo Karen villages transcribe tone on every syllable with Chao numbers (45, 33, 31, 51 seen); data called phonetic, no tone inventory or analysis given.

tone.quote: Standard IPA symbols are used in the transcription of both the word lists and the texts. Diphthongs are transcribed with a raised second element. Tone is transcribed using the Chao tone numbers, where 5 is high and 1 is low. Thus, 45 is a high-rising tone, 33 is a mid-level tone etcetera. Glottalization is marked with a final raised glottal stop. Nasalization is marked with a tilde. All data is phonetic and has not undergone detailed phonological or syntactic analysis.
